items.stem: Rao–Blackwell guarantees that η(T) = E[δ(X) | T] satisfies:
options: η is unbiased and Var(η) ≤ Var(δ), provided T is sufficient
η is the UMVUE, provided T is sufficient
η is unbiased and Var(η) < Var(δ), for any statistic T
η has smaller mean squared error than δ, provided T is complete
items.explanation: Unbiasedness comes from the tower property; the variance inequality from Var(δ) = E[Var(δ|T)] + Var(η). Option C overstates it twice: the inequality is not strict, and T must be sufficient or η is not even a statistic. Option B skips completeness, without which there is no uniqueness and so no UMVUE claim.

items.stem: X₁,…,X₅ are iid Poisson(λ) with ΣXᵢ = 3. The UMVUE of e^(−λ) is ((n−1)/n)^T. Give its value.
items.explanation: ((n−1)/n)^T = (4/5)³ = 0.512. Option C is e^(−0.6), the plug-in estimate e^(−λ̂) with λ̂ = x̄ = 0.6 — a perfectly reasonable estimator but a biased one, and not the UMVUE. Option D is (3/5)³ and option A is x̄ itself.
items.check: The base is (n−1)/n = 4/5, not x̄ and not T/n. Confirm which of n and T goes in the exponent before you compute.

items.stem: Consider Lehmann–Scheffé and the UMVUEs it produces.
items.explanation: A is true — that is the statement. B is false: completeness is required, and without it the theorem is silent. C is true, and is the standard pathology. D is true — the UMVUE is not invariant, unlike the MLE.
statements: If T is complete sufficient and η(T) is unbiased for g(θ), then η(T) is the unique UMVUE.
Sufficiency of T alone is enough for the uniqueness conclusion.
A UMVUE can take values outside the range of the quantity it estimates.
The UMVUE of g(θ) need not equal g applied to the UMVUE of θ.

A.why: The theorem exactly as stated, with uniqueness holding almost surely.

B.why: Without completeness you get Rao–Blackwell's improvement but no uniqueness.

C.why: X̄² − σ²/n can be negative while μ² cannot; (−1)^X estimates a number in (0,1).

D.why: UMVUEs are not invariant. For U(0,θ), the UMVUE of θ² is (n+2)/n·X₍ₙ₎², not the square of the UMVUE of θ.

items.stem: X₁,…,X₆ are iid Bernoulli(p) with ΣXᵢ = 4. The UMVUE of p² is T(T−1)/(n(n−1)). Give its value, and say how it compares with p̂².
items.explanation: T(T−1)/(n(n−1)) = 4·3/(6·5) = 12/30 = 0.400, while p̂² = (4/6)² = 0.444. The plug-in estimator is biased upward for p², and the UMVUE sits below it — which is the correction the (T−1) and (n−1) supply.
items.check: Two parts: the value and the comparison. If you computed only 0.4, confirm p̂² before choosing, because three options carry that same number.

items.stem: For which situation does Lehmann–Scheffé fail to deliver a UMVUE?
options: N(θ, θ²) with θ > 0, where the minimal sufficient statistic is not complete
U(0, θ), where X₍ₙ₎ is complete sufficient
Bernoulli(p), where T = ΣXᵢ is complete sufficient
Poisson(λ), where T = ΣXᵢ is complete sufficient
items.explanation: N(θ,θ²) is a curved exponential family: (ΣXᵢ, ΣXᵢ²) is minimal sufficient but not complete, so the theorem has nothing to act on. A UMVUE may still exist, but Lehmann–Scheffé cannot identify it. The other three are full-rank families whose sufficient statistic is complete.

items.stem: X₁,…,X₈ are iid U(0,θ) with sample maximum x₍₈₎ = 6. Give the UMVUE of θ and the MLE of θ.
items.explanation: The UMVUE is (n+1)/n · x₍ₙ₎ = (9/8)(6) = 6.75; the MLE is x₍ₙ₎ = 6 itself. The UMVUE must exceed the sample maximum, because the maximum can never exceed θ and so understates it. Option C scales the wrong way, making the bias worse.
items.check: The multiplier is (n+1)/n = 9/8, greater than 1. Any answer below the sample maximum is wrong on sight.

items.stem: Let δ be an unbiased estimator of g(θ) and let T be a statistic.
items.explanation: A is false — equality holds whenever δ is already a function of T, so the improvement need not be strict. B is true, by the tower property. C is true, and is the point of requiring sufficiency. D is false: unbiasedness restricts the comparison to unbiased estimators, and a biased estimator can have smaller MSE.
statements: Rao–Blackwellising always strictly reduces the variance.
E[E[δ|T]] = g(θ) whenever δ is unbiased.
If T is not sufficient, E[δ|T] may depend on θ and so may not be a statistic.
A UMVUE has the smallest mean squared error among all estimators.

A.why: It is ≤. Equality when Var(δ|T) = 0, i.e. δ already depends on the data only through T.

B.why: The tower property, needing nothing beyond δ being unbiased.

C.why: Sufficiency is exactly what frees the conditional distribution of θ.

D.why: Smallest variance among UNBIASED estimators only. The MLE of σ² beats s² on MSE.

items.stem: X₁,…,X₆ are iid Exponential with rate λ and Σxᵢ = 24. Give the MLE of λ and the UMVUE of λ.
items.explanation: The MLE is n/Σxᵢ = 6/24 = 0.250. Since E[1/ΣX] = λ/(n−1), the unbiased version is (n−1)/Σxᵢ = 5/24 = 0.2083, and ΣX is complete sufficient so Lehmann–Scheffé makes it the UMVUE. Option C swaps them; option B gives the mean 1/λ rather than the rate.
items.check: The UMVUE is the MLE shrunk by (n−1)/n, so it must be the SMALLER of the two. If your UMVUE came out larger, you scaled the wrong way.

items.stem: X₁,…,X₁₀ are iid N(μ, σ²) with σ² = 5 known, and x̄ = 4. Give the UMVUE of μ².
items.explanation: X̄ is complete sufficient for μ. E[X̄²] = Var(X̄) + μ² = σ²/n + μ², so the UMVUE is x̄² − σ²/n = 16 − 5/10 = 15.5. Option B is x̄² itself, which overstates μ² by σ²/n. Option C subtracts σ² rather than σ²/n.
items.check: The correction is the variance of the MEAN, σ²/n = 0.5, not σ² = 5. Subtracting the wrong one is the commonest slip in this item.

items.stem: To find a UMVUE by Rao–Blackwellisation, arrange these steps in the order they are carried out.
items.explanation: Identify the complete sufficient statistic first — it determines whether the method applies at all and what you will condition on. Then find any unbiased estimator, compute the conditional expectation, and finally invoke Lehmann–Scheffé. Starting by hunting for an unbiased estimator wastes effort if no complete sufficient statistic exists.
items: A. Find any unbiased estimator δ of g(θ), however crude
B. Invoke Lehmann–Scheffé to declare the result the UMVUE
C. Identify a complete sufficient statistic T
D. Compute η(T) = E[δ | T] using the conditional distribution given T

items.stem: The Rao–Blackwell theorem requires that:
options: the loss function is squared error and nothing else
T is complete, so that the conditional expectation is unique
T is sufficient, so that E[δ(X) | T] does not depend on θ
δ is the maximum likelihood estimator
items.explanation: Sufficiency is what makes E[δ(X) | T] a statistic at all — without it the conditional expectation would still involve θ and could not be computed from the data. Completeness is the extra ingredient Lehmann–Scheffé adds to get uniqueness; Rao–Blackwell alone does not need it. The result holds for any convex loss, squared error being the familiar case.

items.stem: X₁,…,X₄ are iid Poisson(λ) with ΣXᵢ = 8. The UMVUE of λ² is T(T−1)/n². Give its value.
items.explanation: T(T−1)/n² = 8(7)/16 = 56/16 = 3.5. The naive x̄² = 2² = 4 is biased upward: E[X̄²] = λ² + λ/n, so the correction subtracts exactly that bias.
items.check: The UMVUE of λ² should come out BELOW x̄², since x̄² overestimates. If yours is larger, the correction has the wrong sign.

items.stem: Consider Rao–Blackwellisation and what it delivers.
items.explanation: A is true — conditioning on a sufficient statistic cannot increase the variance, and strictly decreases it unless δ was already a function of T. B is false: Rao–Blackwell preserves unbiasedness but gives no uniqueness, which is what Lehmann–Scheffé adds. C is true, and it is why the improved estimator is computable. D is true: the result holds for any convex loss, not only squared error.
statements: Var(E[δ|T]) ≤ Var(δ), with equality only when δ is already a function of T.
Rao–Blackwell alone proves the improved estimator is the UMVUE.
E[δ|T] is free of θ because T is sufficient.
The improvement holds for any convex loss function.

A.why: The conditional variance decomposition: Var(δ) = Var(E[δ|T]) + E[Var(δ|T)].

B.why: Uniqueness needs completeness. Rao–Blackwell improves; Lehmann–Scheffé certifies.

C.why: That is exactly what sufficiency buys — the conditional law is parameter-free.

D.why: Jensen's inequality applied conditionally, so convexity is all that is needed.

items.stem: X₁,…,X₉ are iid N(μ, σ²) with σ² = 18 known, and x̄ = 5. The UMVUE of μ² is X̄² − σ²/n. Give its value.
items.explanation: X̄² − σ²/n = 25 − 18/9 = 25 − 2 = 23. The subtraction removes the bias in X̄², since E[X̄²] = μ² + σ²/n. X̄ is complete sufficient for μ, so this unbiased function of it is the UMVUE.
items.check: σ²/n = 2, not σ² = 18. Subtracting the whole variance instead of the variance of the MEAN is the slip the question is built around.

items.stem: Rao–Blackwellising an estimator that is already a function of the complete sufficient statistic:
options: returns the same estimator, with no improvement
is not permitted by the theorem
items.explanation: If δ is already a function of T then E[δ|T] = δ, so nothing changes. That is the equality case of the theorem, and it is also the signal that you have already arrived: an unbiased function of the complete sufficient statistic is the UMVUE and cannot be improved.

items.stem: X₁,…,Xₙ are iid Bernoulli(p), T = ΣXᵢ. Starting from the crude unbiased estimator δ = X₁ of p, compute E[δ | T = t] and identify the resulting estimator.
items.explanation: Given T = t, the t successes are equally likely to sit in any of the n positions, so P(X₁ = 1 | T = t) = t/n. Hence E[X₁ | T = t] = t/n = x̄. Rao–Blackwellising the crudest possible unbiased estimator — look at the first observation only — delivers the sample proportion, and since T is complete sufficient, Lehmann–Scheffé certifies it as the UMVUE.
items.check: Sanity-check unbiasedness at the end: E[T/n] = np/n = p ✓. Option B is the UMVUE of p², not of p.

items.stem: Consider Lehmann–Scheffé in practice.
items.explanation: A is true — that is the theorem's conclusion. B is true: finding ANY unbiased function of the complete sufficient statistic is enough, which is why guessing and correcting works. C is false: a UMVUE need not attain the Cramér–Rao bound, as the exponential rate shows. D is true — without completeness you may have several unbiased functions of T and no way to choose.
statements: An unbiased function of a complete sufficient statistic is the unique UMVUE.
You may find the UMVUE by correcting the bias of any function of T.
The UMVUE produced always attains the Cramér–Rao bound.
Without completeness, the uniqueness conclusion fails.

B.why: Any unbiased function will do — there is only one, so whichever you find is it.

C.why: (n−1)/ΣX has variance λ²/(n−2), strictly above the floor λ²/n.

D.why: Completeness is precisely what rules out a second unbiased function of T.

items.stem: X₁,…,X₁₂ are iid U(0,θ) with x₍₁₂₎ = 9. Give the UMVUE of θ and its variance formula.
items.explanation: X₍ₙ₎ is complete sufficient for θ, and (n+1)X₍ₙ₎/n is its unbiased multiple, so Lehmann–Scheffé makes it the UMVUE: (13/12)(9) = 9.75. Its variance is θ²/(n(n+2)), of order n⁻² — faster than the 1/n rate any regular family could manage, which is possible only because the support depends on θ and the Cramér–Rao conditions fail.
items.check: Two parts here and the second is the one candidates drop. An O(n⁻²) variance is the fingerprint of a boundary-support family.

items.stem: A UMVUE exists and has been found, yet its variance exceeds the Cramér–Rao bound. What does this tell you?
options: A better unbiased estimator exists but has not been found
The UMVUE has been computed incorrectly
Nothing is wrong — the bound need not be attainable, and the UMVUE is still the best unbiased estimator
The regularity conditions must have failed
items.explanation: Being the best unbiased estimator and sitting on the Cramér–Rao floor are different achievements. The bound is attained only when the score factorises as A(θ)[T − g(θ)]; when it does not, the floor is simply unreachable and the UMVUE sits above it. The exponential rate is the standard case: UMVUE variance λ²/(n−2) against a floor of λ²/n.

items.stem: To find a UMVUE by Lehmann–Scheffé, arrange these steps.
items.explanation: Find the complete sufficient statistic first — everything downstream is stated in terms of it. Then verify completeness, since without it the conclusion is only Rao–Blackwell. Then produce some unbiased function of that statistic, and conclude it is the unique UMVUE.
items: A. Produce an unbiased function of that statistic
B. Verify the statistic is complete
C. Identify a sufficient statistic for θ
D. Conclude it is the unique UMVUE
